selection_rule: Every statement by an in-scope officeholder quoted in a story published on Nov. 22 or 23, 2026 in the NPR Politics and PBS NewsHour Politics feeds, as read on Nov. 23 in the early morning ET, less the stories earlier pages already used, plus every transcript from the fixed transcript sources dated in that window (six were: three CBS 60 Minutes segments, NBC Meet the Press, ABC This Week and CNN State of the Union, all Nov. 22). One NPR story, "After midterm losses, Republicans debate what's next for the party," could not be read and is not included. Transcripts from Nov. 16 to 20 were searched only to confirm quotes. PBS NewsHour carries Associated Press reporting. Nine of the fifteen readable stories and transcripts quoted no officeholder in scope. Greetings and procedural remarks, quotes under five words, commentators' accounts of what officials said, and statements by officials outside the offices in scope (including the Director of National Intelligence, senators-elect and former officeholders other than presidents and vice presidents) were left out. Statements are worded as the outlet reported them.
lede: The Sunday shows on Nov. 22 were dominated by the aftermath of the midterm elections, in which Democrats won control of both chambers of Congress, and by a week of technology outages. Sen. John Kennedy of Louisiana and Sen. Chris Van Hollen of Maryland, who is challenging Chuck Schumer for Senate Democratic leader, gave long interviews on NBC's Meet the Press; Rep. Jamie Raskin of Maryland appeared on CNN's State of the Union to discuss House Democrats' plans for investigations.

This page lists every statement by an officeholder in scope that was quoted in the day's stories and transcripts, labelled by kind. Factual statements and the factual premises of predictions are checked one at a time against AskAmerica's warehouse and primary sources; statements still waiting for a check are marked not yet checked.

statements.context: On Meet the Press, on how Nvidia chips reached China, referring to the Commerce Department and U.S. export controls.
statements.quote: that the Department of Commerce has allowed the Communist Party of China to circumvent our export controls on advanced chips
statements.test: True if official records (Commerce Department actions, export licenses, indictments or inspector-general findings) show advanced U.S. chips reached China in breach of or around export controls in a way the Commerce Department permitted or failed to stop. statements.speaker: Chris Van Hollen
statements.context: On Meet the Press, describing a political spending rule in connection with Elon Musk's election spending and federal contracts.
statements.quote: the Elon Musk loophole that allows him to spend hundreds of millions of dollars while he’s getting billions of dollars in contracts
statements.test: True if Elon Musk spent hundreds of millions of dollars on U.S. elections while his companies held billions of dollars in federal contracts, and a rule (a 'loophole') allows a contractor's owner to spend that way. False if Musk's election spending or his companies' federal contracts are far smaller, or if federal law bars such spending. Cannot be determined if it turns on what counts as a 'loophole'.
statements.finding: AskAmerica's data show Musk gave about $359 million to political committees in the 2026 cycle, and SpaceX held about $3.6 billion to $3.8 billion a year in federal contract obligations in fiscal 2024 to 2026, so the dollar figures hold. Whether this is a 'loophole' is a legal reading: 52 U.S.C. 30119 bars contributions by a person who holds a federal contract, and its text does not address an owner giving personal funds.

statements.speaker: Chris Van Hollen
statements.context: On Meet the Press, on whether Congress should fund military operations against Iran.
statements.quote: we should not continue to fund an illegal war that’s driving up prices
statements.test: Premise only: True if price data show the U.S. war with Iran has raised prices for Americans (for example oil, gasoline or overall consumer prices rising with the war). False if prices have not risen, or fell, during the war. Cannot be determined if prices rose but the war's part in it cannot be separated from other causes.
statements.premise: The U.S. war with Iran is driving up prices for Americans.
statements.finding: AskAmerica's EIA data show U.S. regular gasoline rising from $2.94 a gallon on Feb. 23, 2026, days before the war began on Feb. 28, to $3.96 on March 23 and a peak near $4.48; it was still $4.27 on Oct. 26. The consumer price index rose 0.9% in March and 3.1% from February to October, and the Associated Press attributes the March and April jumps to the war and Iran's closing of the Strait of Hormuz.

statements.context: In a clip shown on Meet the Press before he is expected to become House speaker in January 2027.
statements.quote: The status quo is unacceptable.

statements.speaker: Barack Obama
statements.office: Former President of the United States
statements.context: Speaking to incoming House Democrats, in a clip shown on Meet the Press.
statements.quote: Hang onto your values, your commitments, your convictions.

statements.speaker: Marco Rubio
statements.context: Speaking about the week's technology outages and whether they are linked to a coordinated attack, as shown on ABC's This Week.
statements.quote: We have absolutely no reason to believe, we have no evidence, no indications of any kind that these instances -- that these incidents are related to each other.
statements.test: True if U.S. government officials or agencies have publicly found no evidence linking the week's technology outages to one another. False if an official finding links them. Cannot be determined if no official assessment beyond the secretary's own words is available.

also_said.quote: We are not under systemic attack.

statements.speaker: Josh Hawley
statements.context: In a clip shown on ABC's This Week, on whether the week's technology outages were coincidence.
statements.quote: If this is all a coincidence, it’s like the greatest coincidence in the history of the world.

statements.speaker: JD Vance
statements.office: Vice President of the United States
statements.context: Asked whether Americans should prepare for emergencies after the week's technology outages, in a clip shown on ABC's This Week.
statements.quote: Should we be preparing to build a bunker and to stock up on food and water? And my answer to that is, no.

statements.speaker: Donald Trump
statements.context: Speaking to Americans about the week's technology outages and stock market losses, in a clip shown on ABC's This Week.
statements.quote: Tell them to relax. Everything’s good.

statements.speaker: Donald Trump
statements.context: Describing a call with the governor-elect of Texas, in a clip shown on ABC's This Week.
statements.quote: I received a phone call two days ago from the new governor of -- governor-elect of Texas. She was really nice. It was a very productive call. And she wants to have a strong border.
statements.test: True if a record shows Texas's governor-elect called President Trump about two days before his remarks. False if records show no such call or a different date. Cannot be determined if only the president's own account exists.

statements.speaker: Tom Cotton
statements.context: Quoted by ABC's host from an interview with The Wall Street Journal, on Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick and warnings about AI chips smuggled into China.
statements.quote: If Howard Lutnick wanted my support, perhaps he should have responded to my many letters warning about the Chinese communist front companies and, more importantly, taking the threats of communist China more seriously.

source.note: Read aloud by the host from a Wall Street Journal interview; the Journal original was not located.

statements.test: Premise only: True if records show Senator Cotton sent Commerce Secretary Lutnick several letters warning about Chinese communist front companies. False if Cotton sent no such letters to Lutnick. Cannot be determined if letters exist but their recipients or subjects cannot be confirmed.
statements.premise: Senator Cotton sent Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick many letters warning about Chinese communist front companies.

statements.speaker: JD Vance
statements.office: Vice President of the United States
statements.context: Answering a question at a White House news conference on Friday about whether the war with Iran was worth the loss of the Senate.
statements.quote: It's the biggest state sponsor of terrorism.
statements.test: True if the State Department's latest Country Reports on Terrorism or equivalent official statement calls Iran the leading or worst state sponsor of terrorism. False if the official reports rank another country above Iran. Cannot be determined if no official ranking exists.

statements.speaker: JD Vance
statements.office: Vice President of the United States
statements.context: Answering a question at a White House news conference on Friday about the Iran war and the loss of the Senate.
statements.quote: the president has said he would do it again
statements.test: True if President Trump has publicly said he would go to war with Iran again, or would make the same decision again. False if the record shows he said otherwise. Cannot be determined if no such statement by the president can be found.

statements.speaker: JD Vance
statements.office: Vice President of the United States
statements.context: Answering a question at a White House news conference on Friday about his role while President Trump is in office.
statements.quote: my goal is and my job is to support the president of the United States

statements.speaker: Tom Cotton
statements.context: Quoted by CNN's host from an interview with The Wall Street Journal, on the Commerce Department's response to Nvidia chip diversion to China.
statements.quote: It's just a bit late, regrettably, and I think we need to catalog the damage that's been done.

source.note: Read aloud by the host from a Wall Street Journal interview; the Journal original was not located.

statements.speaker: Jamie Raskin
statements.context: On CNN's State of the Union, discussing President Trump's executive order on federal contractors' responses to congressional requests.
statements.quote: Trump is scrambling to cover up all of the corruption, the kickbacks, the bribery, the insider influence.

statements.speaker: Jamie Raskin
statements.context: On CNN's State of the Union, on the legal effect of President Trump's executive order on federal contractors' responses to Congress.
statements.quote: that so-called executive order has all the force of an interoffice memo
statements.test: True if the executive order cannot bind private contractors or Congress, under the Constitution or statute. False if the order has legal force over contractors' responses to Congress. Cannot be determined if it turns on a legal question no court has decided.

statements.speaker: Jamie Raskin
statements.context: On CNN's State of the Union, responding to a letter from a U.S. attorney, on prosecutions the Trump administration has brought.
statements.quote: We know that they illegitimately tried to prosecute James Comey, Letitia James, Adam Schiff, Maggie Goodlander, on and on, on a whole bunch of cases.
statements.test: True if the Justice Department under Trump brought or sought criminal charges against James Comey, Letitia James, Adam Schiff and Maggie Goodlander. False if any of them was never the subject of a federal prosecution or charging effort. Cannot be determined if 'illegitimately' is the point at issue, which is a judgment the records do not settle.

statements.speaker: Jamie Raskin
statements.context: On CNN's State of the Union, on what the Federal Records Act requires of federal officials.
statements.quote: That's called the Federal Records Act, which says that they have got to preserve and document all official communications.
statements.test: True if the Federal Records Act requires federal agencies to preserve and document official communications. False if the Act imposes no such duty. Cannot be determined if it turns on how the Act applies to particular communications.

statements.speaker: Jamie Raskin
statements.context: On CNN's State of the Union, describing information given to House Democrats about the FBI's general counsel.
statements.quote: it turns out we had some people who shared with us the fact that the general counsel, the FBI, was engaged in Signal chats -- these are auto-deleting Signal chats -- with a Trump associate relating to a health care fraud potential prosecution.
statements.test: True if a public record (filing, letter, report) shows the FBI general counsel used auto-deleting Signal chats with a Trump associate about a possible health care fraud prosecution. False if a record shows no such chats took place. Cannot be determined if the claim rests only on unnamed sources House Democrats describe.

statements.speaker: Jamie Raskin
statements.context: On CNN's State of the Union, describing the Trump administration's pardons and political fundraising funds.
statements.quote: we know that they have been pardoning lots of people who are engaged in white-collar fraud and getting money to various political and governmental slush funds that Trump has set up.
statements.test: True if President Trump has pardoned many people convicted of white-collar fraud and records link such clemency to money going to political or government funds tied to Trump. False if few white-collar pardons were granted or no such money link is on record. Cannot be determined if the pardons are confirmed but the money link is not.

statements.speaker: Jamie Raskin
statements.context: On CNN's State of the Union, on a law firm's disclosure of work it did for the Trump administration.
statements.quote: one of the law firms has just revealed that nearly $12 million worth of their associates and partners' time was used by the Trump administration in order to do their work and their projects.
statements.test: True if a law firm has disclosed that nearly $12 million worth of its lawyers' time went to work for the Trump administration. False if the disclosed figure is clearly different. Cannot be determined if no such disclosure is found.

statements.speaker: Jamie Raskin
statements.context: On CNN's State of the Union, on commitments of free legal work the Trump administration obtained from law firms.
statements.quote: they got commitments for up to a billion dollars from all of the law firms that were targeted by this scam by the president.
statements.test: True if the law firms that reached agreements with the Trump administration committed up to about $1 billion in free legal work in total. False if the total committed is clearly different (for example under $800 million or over $1.2 billion). Cannot be determined if no total is available.

statements.speaker: Jamie Raskin
statements.context: On CNN's State of the Union, on what House Democrats will do about law firms' work for the Trump administration.
statements.quote: So we're going to expose this entire scheme.

statements.speaker: Hakeem Jeffries
statements.context: In an interview with The New York Times, shown on CNN's State of the Union, on whether he would negotiate with White House chief of staff Stephen Miller.
statements.quote: I have made clear that Stephen Miller's a stone-cold racist.

source.note: Shown as a clip from a New York Times interview; the Times original was not located.

statements.speaker: Donald Trump
statements.context: Speaking about House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries and White House chief of staff Stephen Miller, in a clip shown on CNN's State of the Union.
statements.quote: I look forward to working with Hakeem.

statements.speaker: Donald Trump
statements.context: In a Sunday morning post read aloud on CNN's State of the Union, on Chuck Schumer's possible election as Senate majority leader.
statements.quote: He failed badly as leader once before, one of the worst in history

source.note: Read aloud by the host from a post by the President; the original post was not located.
